quiz.q: What does calling an `async fn` actually do?
options: Runs its body immediately and returns the result
Returns a future — inert work that runs nothing until it is awaited or driven
Blocks until the work is done
quiz.explain: An async fn returns a future. Its body does not run when you call it; something must `.await` it (or a runtime must drive it) for anything to happen.
`.await` is only legal inside async code, because it needs the async state machine around it. In a normal function you hand the future to a runtime instead.

quiz.q: Rust the language ships `async`/`.await`. What does it NOT ship?
options: An executor/runtime to actually drive futures
The ability to define async functions
quiz.explain: Rust provides the syntax and the Future trait but no executor. You pick a runtime like Tokio to drive your top-level future to completion.

quiz.q: Which workload is async best suited for?
options: I/O-bound work with lots of waiting (network, disk), where one thread juggles many tasks
Anything, it's always faster than threads
Only single-step programs with no waiting
quiz.explain: Async shines for I/O-bound work: tasks spend most of their time waiting, so one thread can handle thousands. CPU-bound crunching is better served by threads.

flashcards.back: A future — a value representing work that will produce a result later. It runs nothing until awaited or driven by a runtime.
Drives a future to completion; if it must wait on I/O it parks the task and lets other tasks run, resuming when ready. Only usable inside async code.
Lets `main` be `async`, starts the Tokio runtime, and drives your top-level future — without a runtime, async code never actually runs.
Async = I/O-bound waiting (many idle tasks on few threads). Threads = CPU-bound work across cores.
